analysis.one_liner: Guarantees overtime pay to salaried workers whose salaries fall below a rising threshold.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2026 with 34 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where the record shows no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets employers deny overtime pay to salaried workers classified as executive, administrative, or professional, and the salary cutoff for that exemption has lagged far behind wages. This bill writes a rising minimum-salary threshold into law: $45,000 at first, then $55,000, $65,000, and $75,000 in successive years, after which the threshold automatically rises with the 55th percentile of national salaried earnings. It also tightens the duties test so retail and service managers who spend more than a fifth of their time on ordinary floor work can no longer be denied overtime.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers who are currently classified as exempt from overtime because of their job title but who earn less than the new thresholds. Under the bill they must either be paid time-and-a-half for hours over 40 or be raised above the threshold, which puts more money in the pockets of lower-paid supervisors, office staff, and retail and restaurant managers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Lower-paid salaried managers and office workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes a salary at or above a set threshold a condition of the executive, administrative, and professional overtime exemption, starting at $45,000 and rising to $55,000, $65,000, and $75,000 over four years [S2].

After 2030, the threshold automatically resets each year to the 55th percentile of national weekly earnings for full-time salaried workers, so it keeps pace with wages without Congress having to act again [S2].

It tightens the duties test for retail and service establishments: an exempt employee may spend no more than 20 percent of the time on nonexempt work, down from the current 40 percent, so working supervisors cannot be classified out of overtime pay [S2].
The Bureau of Labor Statistics must publish quarterly public data on weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers by census region, which supports enforcement and transparency [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently pay salaried workers below the thresholds — retail chains, restaurants, small businesses, and office employers — would owe overtime for hours over 40 or would have to raise salaries above the cutoff. Those added labor costs are the direct price of the bill.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face sharply higher labor costs, and small businesses and nonprofits in particular could respond by converting salaried jobs to hourly ones, capping hours, or trimming headcount rather than paying overtime [S2].

The threshold quadruples its climb over four years and then updates automatically without new rulemaking or congressional review, which critics would call an abdication of oversight and a risk of overshooting in a weak economy [S2].

The stricter 20 percent duties limit reduces flexibility for retail and service managers who routinely split time between supervising and hands-on work, and would force many of them onto hourly schedules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — guaranteed overtime for millions of salaried workers who now work extra hours unpaid — is substantial and targeted at the lower end of the salary scale. The costs fall on employers, and the steepest concern is the automatic escalator: tying the threshold to the 55th percentile of salaried earnings with no regular congressional check means a future downturn could squeeze employers who cannot flex the threshold down. The phase-in schedule moderates but does not eliminate that risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on May 15, 2026, joined by 22 other original cosponsors [S2].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which is the only action listed in its history [S4].
The bill has 34 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats [S3].
With the Congress in session through early January 2027, the bill could still move, but a bill with no committee action months after referral is the profile of legislation that does not advance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay salaried workers below the current exemption cutoff keep the existing rules and avoid the added overtime liability the bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 34 cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor appears in the record; the House's Republican majority controls the committee calendar.

industries.note: The bill directly targets the retail/service exemption these employers rely on, capping nonexempt duties at 20 percent so working supervisors must be paid overtime. Their interest in keeping the current 40 percent test runs against workers who want paid overtime.

industries.industry: Employers of lower-paid salaried staff (restaurants, small businesses, office employers)
industries.note: These employers would owe overtime or higher salaries for their exempt staff earning under the thresholds. The cost falls on them as wages and overtime pay flow to workers.

industries.industry: Salaried workers currently classified as exempt
industries.note: Workers earning under the new thresholds gain either overtime pay or a raise. Their interest and the public's interest in accurate pay run together here.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in committee for months with no action, and its support is entirely from House Democrats in a chamber where Republicans hold a majority and control the Education and Workforce calendar. The usual path from here is that it never receives a markup or floor vote and dies at the end of the Congress, as most single-party labor bills do.
